scenario_stem:
Meadowsweet Skincare is a private limited company founded 4 years ago, producing organic facial moisturisers from a small workshop in the capital region. Annual sales reached $410,000 last year through 3 high-street beauty shops. The founder, Priya Nair, bottles 1,800 units a month and believes the brand is ready for online sales.

An online marketplace offers to sell her moisturisers for a 5% commission plus a 3% delivery fee. A nationwide supermarket chain has offered shelf space in 25 stores, ordering 2,400 units a month at $9 per unit, paying 60 days late and charging $1,200 a year in listing fees. Her own website would cost $6,800 to build and promote. The directors must decide which channel of distribution best protects margins and supports growth.

questions.question_text: Define 'retailer'.
questions.model_answer: A retailer is a business that buys goods from producers or wholesalers and sells them in small quantities to final consumers [2].

knowledge_max_2: sells goods to final consumers in small quantities
buys from producers/wholesalers rather than manufacturing

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Meadowsweet Skincare might sell through the supermarket chain.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Supermarkets attract very large numbers of shoppers [k], so shelf space in 25 stores would expose her moisturisers to far more buyers than 3 high-street beauty shops [app]. Reason 2: Supermarkets are trusted, convenient places to buy everyday items [k], and an order of 2,400 units a month at $9 per unit would give a predictable, regular flow of revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: supermarkets reach many/more customers (wider exposure)
regular bulk orders give predictable demand and revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Meadowsweet Skincare would face by selling through supermarkets.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The supermarket pays 60 days late [k], so selling 2,400 units a month at $9 per unit means waiting 2 months for around $21,600 in income [app], which could create cash-flow difficulties [an]. Problem 2: Supermarkets squeeze suppliers on price [k], charging $1,200 a year in listing fees on top of a low unit price [app], reducing the profit available to reinvest in the brand [an].

knowledge_max_2: late payment/long credit terms strain cash flow
supermarkets negotiate low prices and may charge listing fees
analysis_max_2: cash-flow difficulties paying suppliers/wages
lower margins reduce funds for marketing and growth

questions.question_text: Do you think Meadowsweet Skincare should launch its own website to sell directly to consumers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Selling direct through its own website would give Meadowsweet Skincare full control over pricing, branding and customer data [k], avoiding the supermarket's 60-day late payment and $1,200 a year listing fees on the 2,400-unit monthly order [app], allowing more profit to be reinvested in marketing and quality [an]. However, a supermarket chain would give her instant access to shoppers in 25 stores [k], and an order of 2,400 units a month at $9 per unit would generate around $21,600 a month before fees [app], which a new website with unknown traffic may take years to match [an]. Overall, launching her own website is the better option [eval] because the $6,800 build cost is small next to a year's listing fees and it builds a direct customer relationship the brand needs [eval], while she can still approach supermarkets later with better terms.

knowledge_max_2: direct channel gives control of price, brand and customer relationships
indirect channel gives instant reach and sales volume through established retailers
analysis_max_2: more profit reinvested and stronger brand without intermediaries
a new website may take years to match supermarket volume
evaluation_max_2: weighs control/independence against instant supermarket reach
justified recommendation tied to the $6,800 build cost and listing fees

scenario_stem:
Copperdell Outdoor Furniture is a partnership manufacturing hardwood garden dining sets in a workshop employing 18 carpenters. Each set costs $410 to make and sells for $720 through 35 independent retailers, who keep a 28% margin. Delivering to east-region customers by lorry costs $85 per set, a charge Copperdell absorbs on 220 sets a year.

A national wholesaler has offered to buy 750 sets a year at $470 each and collect from the factory, removing all delivery risk. The wholesaler would resell the sets under its own brand in 120 shops. Alternatively, Copperdell could launch a website and sell direct to households, keeping the full price but paying lorry costs of $85 each way and risking returns of 90 kg sets. The partners must decide.

questions.question_text: Define 'wholesaler'.
questions.model_answer: A wholesaler is a business that buys goods in bulk from producers or manufacturers and sells them in smaller quantities to retailers [2].

knowledge_max_2: buys goods in bulk from producers/manufacturers
sells in smaller quantities to retailers/other businesses

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Copperdell Outdoor Furniture might accept the wholesaler's offer.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The wholesaler would collect the sets from the factory [k], so Copperdell could stop absorbing the $85 lorry cost on 220 sets a year [app]. Reason 2: The wholesaler guarantees a regular bulk order [k], buying 750 sets a year at $470 each and reselling them in 120 shops [app].

knowledge_max_2: wholesaler takes over transport/delivery from the factory
regular bulk orders give steady, predictable demand

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Copperdell Outdoor Furniture of selling direct through a website.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Selling direct removes the retailers' 28% margin [k], so Copperdell keeps the full $720 per set instead of sharing the price with 35 independent retailers [app], increasing the profit per set available to reinvest in the workshop [an]. Benefit 2: Selling direct builds a direct relationship with households [k], letting Copperdell collect feedback on its hardwood sets from buyers nationwide [app], which can improve future designs and strengthen loyalty [an].

knowledge_max_2: direct sales keep the full price/higher margin per unit
direct contact builds customer relationships and feedback
analysis_max_2: more profit per set to reinvest in the workshop
feedback improves designs and loyalty

questions.question_text: Do you think Copperdell Outdoor Furniture should accept the wholesaler's contract rather than launch its own website? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the wholesaler would remove all delivery risk [k], guaranteeing collection of 750 sets a year at $470 each and ending the $85 lorry charge absorbed on 220 sets a year [app], giving steady cash flow to run the workshop of 18 carpenters [an]. However, selling direct keeps the full $720 price and avoids the 28% retailer margin [k], and would build direct household customers rather than let the wholesaler resell under its own brand in 120 shops [app], protecting Copperdell's brand identity and long-term margin [an]. Overall, accepting the wholesaler is the safer short-term option [eval] because a guaranteed order of 750 sets a year outweighs the higher online price for a firm currently paying $85 lorry costs [eval], although a website could be added once cash flow improves.

knowledge_max_2: wholesaler gives a guaranteed order and removes transport risk
direct sales keep the full price and the brand
analysis_max_2: steady cash flow lowers risk for the workshop
risk of losing brand identity to the reseller's own brand
evaluation_max_2: weighs guaranteed wholesaler order against higher direct margins
justified recommendation tied to the $85 lorry burden

scenario_stem:
Crimson Chilli Foods is a private limited company in the coastal city producing Crimson Reaper Hot Sauce in 250ml glass bottles. It sells 4,500 bottles a week locally at $5.20 each and wants to enter 2 neighbouring countries. The owner, Daniel Okoro, needs to choose a channel for exporting to foreign buyers.

An export agent based at the northern port offers to find buyers for a 9% commission on completed orders only. Crimson Chilli would remain responsible for shipping and import paperwork. A foreign wholesaler offers to buy 60,000 bottles a year at $3.40 each, collected monthly from the factory. That price is below the local wholesale rate of $3.75, but the deal transfers all transport risk and gives a steady order book. Daniel must decide between the two channels.

questions.question_text: Define 'agent'.
questions.model_answer: An agent is a person or business that acts on behalf of a producer or seller to sell goods in a market, usually in return for a commission, without taking ownership of the goods [2].

knowledge_max_2: acts on behalf of the producer/seller
earns commission and does not own the goods

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Crimson Chilli Foods might export through the agent.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The agent works on commission [k], so Crimson Chilli pays 9% only on completed orders, never on unsold stock [app]. Reason 2: The agent is based at the northern port [k], giving access to buyers in the 2 neighbouring countries without setting up overseas [app].

knowledge_max_2: commission is paid only on completed sales
agent has local knowledge/contacts in foreign markets

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Crimson Chilli Foods of accepting the wholesaler's offer.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The wholesaler would buy 60,000 bottles a year at $3.40 [k], adding a confirmed export order on top of the 4,500 bottles sold locally each week [app], making production planning easier [an]. Benefit 2: The wholesaler collects the bottles monthly from the factory [k], so Crimson Chilli avoids shipping costs, transport risk and import paperwork [app], protecting its local operation's margins [an].

knowledge_max_2: wholesaler provides a large regular order
wholesaler takes on transport and collection risk
analysis_max_2: confirmed order eases production planning and scheduling
no shipping costs/paperwork/risk to manage

questions.question_text: Do you think Crimson Chilli Foods should export through the agent rather than the wholesaler? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The agent would charge only 9% commission on completed orders [k], keeping Crimson Chilli in full control of its price, brand and paperwork in the 2 neighbouring countries [app], preserving the margin on each of the 4,500 bottles it could sell each week and beyond [an]. However, the wholesaler offers a guaranteed 60,000 bottles a year at $3.40 with monthly collection from the factory [k], removing all transport risk and giving a predictable export order Daniel Okoro can plan around [app], which would support investment in extra production capacity [an]. Overall, the agent is the better first step into the export market [eval] because it limits financial risk while the firm tests demand in the 2 new countries [eval], although the wholesaler may suit the firm once the market is proven.

knowledge_max_2: agent = low-risk market testing, commission-only payment
wholesaler = guaranteed volume with transport risk passed on
analysis_max_2: keeps control, margins and brand while testing markets
guaranteed volume supports planning and investment
evaluation_max_2: weighs agent's lower risk against the wholesaler's guaranteed order
justified recommendation tied to testing the two new markets

scenario_stem:
Foxhollow Dairy Farm is a family partnership milking 120 cows and bottling 3,200 litres a week. A refrigerated van delivers to 3 village shops, and 30% of output goes to retail supermarkets at $0.85 per litre, but they return unsold cartons and pay 30 days late. The family is considering selling more through a farm gate shop and a simple website at $1.60 per litre.

A regional wholesaler has offered to collect 4,000 litres a week at $0.95 per litre but requires a $14,000 bottling-line upgrade. Farm gate customers pay up front and receive next-day delivery for $4 per order, yet weekend sales have averaged only 900 litres a week. The family must decide which channel keeps the milk fresh and profitable.

questions.question_text: Define 'direct selling'.
questions.model_answer: Direct selling is when a producer sells its goods straight to the final customer without using any intermediary such as a wholesaler or retailer [2].

knowledge_max_2: producer sells straight to the final consumer
no intermediary (wholesaler/retailer) involved

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Foxhollow Dairy Farm of selling through its own farm gate shop and website.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The farm keeps the full $1.60 per litre [k], almost double the $0.85 per litre that retail supermarkets pay [app]. Reason 2: Farm gate customers pay up front [k], so the farm avoids the 30-day wait for supermarket payment and the cost of returned unsold cartons [app].

knowledge_max_2: producer keeps the full price/no share taken by intermediaries
immediate/up-front payment improves cash flow

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of accepting the wholesaler's offer.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The wholesaler would collect 4,000 litres a week [k], more than the 3,200 litres the farm currently bottles, so spare capacity on the refrigerated van would be used [app], increasing total weekly revenue [an]. Benefit 2: The wholesaler pays $0.95 per litre [k], which is higher than the $0.85 per litre supermarkets pay [app], improving the return on every litre collected [an].

knowledge_max_2: wholesaler offers a larger, more stable weekly volume
wholesaler pays more than the supermarkets
analysis_max_2: spare capacity is used, raising total revenue
better price improves margin per litre

questions.question_text: Do you think Foxhollow Dairy Farm should accept the wholesaler's offer rather than expand direct selling? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The wholesaler offers to collect 4,000 litres a week at $0.95 per litre [k], using the 800 litres of spare capacity and paying more than the $0.85 supermarkets pay [app], providing stable, growing revenue after the $14,000 upgrade [an]. However, direct selling at $1.60 per litre nearly doubles the price per litre [k], and customers pay up front with $4 delivery per order [app], building cash flow and brand loyalty that a wholesaler cannot match [an]. Overall, the farm should accept the wholesaler [eval] because 4,000 litres at $0.95 (around $3,800 a week) beats direct sales of 900 litres at $1.60 (around $1,440 a week) while weekend demand remains small [eval], keeping the farm gate shop open for loyal customers.

knowledge_max_2: wholesaler gives volume, capacity use and stable revenue
direct selling gives a higher price and up-front payment
analysis_max_2: stable growing revenue using spare capacity
direct selling builds cash flow and loyalty but demand is limited
evaluation_max_2: quantified comparison: about $3,800 vs $1,440 a week
justified recommendation linked to weekend demand of 900 litres

scenario_stem:
VoltEdge Electronics is a private limited company operating 2 high-street shops selling televisions, laptops and small appliances. Last year revenue was $1.9 million, with online sales of $640,000 through its own website. Only 4 in 10 computer buyers say they trust paying online without seeing the product first, and 18% of online orders are returned within 14 days.

Nationwide online rivals charge lower prices and offer 24/7 ordering. Switching to online-only would save $220,000 a year in rent and wages but lose the walk-in trade worth $1.26 million last year. Delivering a 55-inch television costs $120 per unit, and many customers complain about delivery times. The owners must decide whether to close the 2 shops and trade online only, or keep both channels open.

questions.question_text: State two benefits of e-commerce for businesses.
questions.model_answer: Businesses can sell to a wider market, reaching customers across the country or the world [1], and businesses can trade 24/7 without the costs of running staffed physical shops at all hours [1].

knowledge_max_2: wider market reach (national/worldwide sales)
trades 24/7/lower overheads than physical shops

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for VoltEdge Electronics of switching to online-only sales.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Trading online only would remove the shops' fixed costs [k], saving $220,000 a year in rent and wages [app]. Reason 2: A website is open at all hours [k], serving customers nationwide and supporting the $640,000 of online revenue already achieved [app].

knowledge_max_2: online-only removes high fixed costs of physical shops
24/7 trading reaches a wider market

questions.question_text: Explain two problems VoltEdge Electronics would face by closing its 2 shops.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Customers cannot see or test products before buying online [k], and only 4 in 10 buyers trust paying online without seeing the item first [app], so demand for televisions and laptops could fall [an]. Problem 2: Bulky televisions cost $120 per unit to deliver [k], and 18% of online orders are returned within 14 days [app], adding delivery and returns costs that erode margins [an].

knowledge_max_2: customers cannot see/test before purchase (trust issue)
delivery and returns add costs
analysis_max_2: demand for high-value goods may fall
delivery and returns costs reduce profit

questions.question_text: Do you think VoltEdge Electronics should close its 2 shops and trade online only? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Closing the 2 shops would save $220,000 a year in rent and wages [k] and let VoltEdge trade 24/7 nationwide, building on the $640,000 of online revenue already achieved [app], raising profit and freeing cash for marketing [an]. However, the shops generated $1.26 million of sales last year [k], and closing them would lose test-before-buy customers, only 4 in 10 of whom trust paying online, facing $120 delivery charges on 55-inch televisions and an 18% return rate [app], likely cutting total revenue by far more than the $220,000 saving [an]. Overall, VoltEdge should keep both channels [eval] because losing $1.26 million of walk-in revenue to save $220,000 is a poor trade [eval], while growing the website alongside the shops.

knowledge_max_2: online-only saves fixed costs and allows 24/7 national reach
shops provide test-before-buy and customer trust
analysis_max_2: higher profit and freed cash for marketing
lost walk-in revenue likely exceeds the saving
evaluation_max_2: weighs the $220,000 saving against $1.26 million shop revenue
justified recommendation to keep both channels

scenario_stem:
Citybasket Grocery is a private limited company running 3 neighbourhood supermarkets and an online delivery service launched 18 months ago. The average online basket is $54, and each van route costs $68 in fuel, driver wages and boxes. Customers pay a $5 delivery charge, but 60% abandon their basket when they see the fee.

The owners propose a $65 minimum order for free delivery within 8 kilometres instead of the $5 charge. Fuel prices have risen 19% this year, and 240 deliveries are made weekly, only 80 of them worth $65 or more. Driver wages absorb half of route costs, and complaints about delivery punctuality rose 15% last month. The owners must decide whether the new rule protects margins or drives away online customers.

questions.question_text: Define 'logistics'.
questions.model_answer: Logistics is the planning and management of the movement and storage of goods, including transport, warehousing and delivery from producer to consumer [2].

knowledge_max_2: planning/managing the movement of goods
includes transport, warehousing and delivery

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Citybasket Grocery of offering free delivery on orders above $65.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Free delivery encourages customers to add items to their basket [k], lifting the average $54 order toward $65 or more [app]. Reason 2: Larger orders spread the $68 delivery cost across more items [k], improving the margin on each of the 240 deliveries made weekly [app].

knowledge_max_2: free delivery incentivises larger baskets
larger orders dilute the fixed cost of delivery

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Citybasket Grocery would face with the $65 free-delivery rule.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Only 80 of them reach $65 or more among the 240 deliveries made weekly [k], so two-thirds of current customers would not qualify for free delivery [app], risking lost orders and more abandoned baskets [an]. Problem 2: Fuel prices have risen 19% this year and driver wages absorb half of route costs [k], so a $65 order may not cover the $68 cost of each route [app], wiping out the delivery margin [an].

knowledge_max_2: most current orders fall below the threshold
free delivery can cost more than it returns on marginal orders
analysis_max_2: two-thirds of customers lose the incentive, orders fall
delivery margin is wiped out as costs exceed revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Citybasket Grocery should introduce the $65 minimum for free delivery? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Free delivery above $65 would encourage customers to add more to their average $54 basket [k], increasing revenue per delivery and helping to cover the $68 route cost [app], so the online channel could become profitable as basket sizes grow [an]. However, only 80 of them reach $65 or more among the 240 weekly deliveries [k], so two-thirds of customers gain nothing, and with 60% already abandoning baskets at the $5 charge, some may switch to rivals [app], risking a fall in delivery volume [an]. Overall, the owners should introduce the $65 rule [eval] because raising basket sizes is the best lever to offset the 19% fuel cost rise [eval], provided they monitor abandoned baskets closely after the change.

knowledge_max_2: a free-delivery minimum lifts average basket size
many orders below the threshold risk lost volume
analysis_max_2: bigger baskets cover route costs, lifting profit
abandonment and rival switching may cut volume
evaluation_max_2: weighs basket-size incentive against two-thirds not qualifying
recommendation tied to offsetting the 19% fuel cost rise

scenario_stem:
Petalpost Florists is a partnership running 2 shops in the commercial district, selling bouquets for birthdays, weddings and everyday gifts. Walk-in bouquets average $46, while online orders average $52 but 12% are refunded within 48 hours because the flowers arrive bruised or smaller than the photographs suggest. Each courier delivery costs the firm $7. Online sales now account for 40% of monthly bouquet revenue.

The spring wedding season will bring 340 online bouquets over the next 3 months. Online buyers cannot see or touch the flowers before dispatch, and 9 complaints last month mentioned misleading photos. A competitor has been accused of buying fake reviews, which the partners refuse to do. The partners must decide whether to keep promoting delivery or concentrate on the 2 shops.

questions.question_text: Define 'intermediary'.
questions.model_answer: An intermediary is a person or business, such as a wholesaler, retailer or agent, that links the producer of a product with the final consumer in the channel of distribution [2].

knowledge_max_2: links producer to final consumer
examples: wholesaler, retailer or agent

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Petalpost Florists of promoting online bouquet orders.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Online orders average $52 per bouquet [k], which is $6 more than the $46 walk-in average [app]. Reason 2: A website is open all day and night [k], capturing sales during the spring wedding season, which will bring 340 online bouquets over the next 3 months [app].

knowledge_max_2: online orders have a higher average value
24/7 availability widens exposure and sales

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages for Petalpost Florists of delivering online orders.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Online buyers cannot see or touch the flowers before dispatch [k], and 12% are refunded within 48 hours because the flowers arrive bruised or smaller than the photographs suggest [app], adding courier and refund costs [an]. Disadvantage 2: Each courier delivery costs the firm $7 [k], while 9 complaints last month mentioned misleading photos [app], damaging the firm's reputation and future sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: customers cannot see/touch before buying
refunds and damaged goods erode margins
analysis_max_2: refund and courier costs reduce profit
reputation suffers from misleading photos/complaints

questions.question_text: Do you think Petalpost Florists should keep promoting online delivery rather than concentrate on its 2 shops? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Keeping delivery would exploit the 40% of monthly bouquet revenue already coming online at an average of $52 per order [k], capturing the 340 wedding bouquets over the coming 3 months with round-the-clock ordering [app], growing sales beyond what the 2 shops can handle [an]. However, 12% of online orders are refunded within 48 hours and each delivery costs $7 [k], while online buyers cannot see or touch the flowers and 9 complaints mentioned misleading photos [app], eroding profit and risking the reputational damage that fake-review accusations against rivals also show [an]. Overall, Petalpost should keep promoting delivery while tightening quality control [eval] because higher online revenue outweighs refund costs if it photographs honestly and packs carefully [eval], while refusing to buy fake reviews at all times.

knowledge_max_2: online channel already substantial and higher value
refunds, delivery cost and reputation risks
analysis_max_2: sales beyond physical capacity/24-7 ordering
margin erosion and reputational damage
evaluation_max_2: weighs online growth against refund and reputation risks
justified recommendation tied to honest photography and quality control

scenario_stem:
Nettlemead Jewellery is a sole trader business handcrafting silver rings and earrings from a workshop in the market town. Elena Marchetti sells about 210 pieces a month at $48 each through craft fairs and 2 boutique gift shops, which pay her $26 per piece wholesale. She is considering selling online.

An online marketplace charging 15% commission plus $300 a month would reach 3 million registered buyers, but her pieces would sit alongside 900 similar sellers. Her own website would cost $2,400 to build, with 2% card fees and full control over branding, but she estimates only 60 visitors a day. Six loyal customers have said they would not buy jewellery online without seeing it in person. Elena must decide which online route grows sales.

questions.question_text: State two limitations of selling through an online marketplace.
questions.model_answer: The marketplace charges a commission on every sale [1], and the seller's products appear alongside many competing sellers, reducing control over branding and pricing [1].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Nettlemead Jewellery of joining the online marketplace.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The marketplace reaches 3 million registered buyers [k], giving far wider exposure than craft fairs and 2 boutique gift shops [app]. marketplace provides infrastructure and traffic

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Nettlemead Jewellery of building its own website.

Benefit 2: A personal website gives full control over branding and presentation [k], letting her tell her handcrafted story to buyers instead of competing with 900 similar sellers [app], strengthening loyalty and repeat purchases [an].

knowledge_max_2: lower selling costs/no commission
full control of brand and customer experience
analysis_max_2: more profit per piece at volume
stronger brand differentiation and loyalty

questions.question_text: Do you think Nettlemead Jewellery should build its own website rather than join the marketplace? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Her own website would avoid the 15% commission and $300 a month [k], saving about $7.20 per $48 piece, roughly $1,500 a month on 210 pieces [app], keeping more margin and full control of her brand and customer list [an]. However, the marketplace offers 3 million ready buyers compared with her estimate of 60 visitors a day on a new site [k], and six loyal customers have said they would not buy jewellery online without seeing it first [app], so a personal site may mean slow sales and a poor return on the $2,400 build cost [an]. Overall, Elena should build her own website but keep selling at craft fairs [eval], because the $1,500 monthly commission saving compounds quickly against a one-off $2,400 build cost [eval], while the fairs supply the traffic a new site needs.

scenario_stem:
Gleamwheels Mobile Car Wash is a private limited company founded 3 years ago, washing an average of 620 cars a month at $18 each from 2 vans. The owner, Sam Whitmore, promotes the business through leaflets and a simple booking form. A chain of 4 car dealerships has offered to refer customers in exchange for 25% of each sale, bringing an estimated 150 extra washes a month.

Dealership referrals would give Gleamwheels steady weekday work with no extra advertising spend, and the dealers could promote the service at vehicle handover. However, Gleamwheels would keep only $13.50 per $18 wash through this channel, and Sam fears dependence on 1 partner. His own booking app would cost $3,900 plus $110 a month, and 45% of current customers already book by phone. Sam must decide which route to take.

Overall, Gleamwheels should accept the referral offer short-term [eval] because immediate extra weekday volume at zero marketing cost beats waiting for an unproven app to attract users [eval], while keeping the app as a longer-term goal to cut commission dependence.

scenario_stem:
Cobbled Lane Books is a private limited company running 1 independent bookshop in an old market building. Annual sales reached $680,000, and 30% of revenue now comes from an online marketplace charging 14% commission on every sale. The shop's monthly events attract about 900 visitors, and 55% of past buyers belong to its free email club.
